Main Provisions of the EU AI Act

The EU AI Act is the world's first comprehensive regulatory framework for artificial intelligence, designed to ensure trustworthy AI development while protecting fundamental rights. It takes a risk-based approach, with different obligations depending on the level of risk posed by AI systems.

Risk-Based Categories

Risk Level — What It Covers — Requirements
Unacceptable Risk — AI that manipulates behavior, real-time facial recognition in public spaces, social scoring systems, and systems generating non-consensual sexual content or child exploitation material — Banned (with limited exemptions)
High-Risk — AI used in hiring, education, critical infrastructure, biometrics, border control, and other sensitive areas — Conformity assessments, transparency, quality assurance, human oversight, post-market surveillance
Limited-Risk — Chatbots and other AI with some risks to users — Transparency obligations only (disclosure that it's AI)
Minimal-Risk — Most AI systems with negligible risk — No specific regulations

General-Purpose AI (GPAI) Requirements

The Act includes special rules for foundation models and large generative AI systems like ChatGPT. Open-source models have reduced requirements, while closed-source models must provide transparency documentation. High-impact models (those trained with exceptional computational power) face additional evaluation requirements to assess systemic risks.  [1]

Other Key Provisions

Governance and enforcement: The EU must establish an AI Board and national competent authorities to oversee compliance, with the EU AI Office centralizing oversight of general-purpose AI systems.  [2]

Innovation support: The Act creates regulatory sandboxes where companies can test AI solutions in controlled environments before full deployment.  [1]

Penalties: Non-compliance carries significant fines of up to €35 million or 7% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher.  [3]

Implementation Timeline

The Act entered into force on 1 August 2024, but requirements apply in phases:

Date — What Takes Effect
2 February 2025 — Prohibitions on unacceptable-risk AI (social scoring, facial recognition bans, deepfakes/CSAM) and AI literacy obligations
2 August 2025 — General-purpose AI obligations and governance structures (Member States designate authorities, EU board established)
2 August 2026 — Transparency rules and enforcement begins; majority of the Act's main rules apply
2 December 2026 — New prohibitions on deepfakes and CSAM take effect
2 August 2027 — Regulatory sandboxes become operational in Member States
2 December 2027 — High-risk AI systems in sensitive areas (Annex III) must comply
2 August 2028 — High-risk AI embedded in regulated products (lifts, toys, etc.) must comply

 [1]

The Digital Omnibus amendments (which entered into force on 27 July 2026) simplified implementation by extending some deadlines and clarifying rules to reduce complexity for businesses while maintaining strong protections.  [1]
